abstract: Whitepaper by Sania Edlich and Torsten Sløk of Apollo Global Management estimating the wage and employment effects of AI adoption across US occupations. Its methodological contribution is substituting observed usage data from the Anthropic Economic Index for the theoretical exposure measures (Felten, Webb, Eloundou et al.) that dominate prior work, on the argument that what AI is actually being used for is a better treatment variable than what it could in principle do. Using a difference-in-differences design with occupation and year fixed effects across 321 matched occupations from 2015 to 2025, the authors find that high-exposure occupations experienced real wage growth 6.7 percentage points slower after 2023 with no detectable employment effect, and read this as firms capturing AI productivity gains through wage compression rather than workforce reduction. The effect is regressive: it concentrates in the bottom of the wage distribution and among service occupations, while top earners show no significant effect. The authors put a conservative lower-bound on aggregate labor income loss at $28 billion annually across the 5.8 million workers in high-exposure occupations.
keyFindings: Workers in high-exposure occupations saw real wage growth about 6.7 percentage points slower than workers in low-exposure occupations after 2023 (Table 3 coefficient -0.0667, SE 0.0181, statistically significant).

No significant employment effect was found from an occupation having a high AI exposure score (coefficient -0.0639, SE 0.0870, not significant), which the authors interpret as wage compression rather than workforce reduction.
5.8 million US workers are in high-exposure occupations, about 3.7 percent of the US labor force, where high exposure means an Anthropic Economic Index usage score of 0.5 or above.

The bottom quartile of the wage distribution saw real wage growth decline about 10.7 percent relative to low-exposure occupations, versus 5.4 percent in the second quartile and 4.0 percent in the third; the top quartile showed no statistically significant effect.
Service occupations saw real wage growth fall about 24.3 percent relative to low-exposure occupations after 2023, the largest estimated effect in the paper.
Management and professional occupations saw real wage growth fall 4.1 percent relative to non-exposed peers; blue-collar workers showed no statistically significant effects.
Conservative lower-bound estimate of aggregate labor income loss is $28 billion annually across the 5.8 million affected workers.
methodology: Difference-in-differences with occupation and year fixed effects: log(RealWage_it) = alpha + beta(Post_t x AnthropicExposure_i) + gamma_i + delta_t + epsilon_it. Treatment is a binary high-exposure indicator set at an Anthropic Economic Index observed-usage score of 0.5 or above; Post is 2024 onward. Wage and employment data come from BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, 2015 to 2025, across 321 occupations successfully matched to the Anthropic index, giving 3,296 occupation-year observations. Standard errors are clustered by occupation. Adjusted R-squared is 0.991 for the employment specification and 0.989 for the wage specification. Table 6 reports robustness at alternative exposure cutoffs of 0.4 and 0.6.
qualifiers: Tier 2: asset-manager research, not peer-reviewed and not a government statistical release, though the design is conventional and fully specified. The treatment variable inherits whatever selection is present in Anthropic Economic Index traffic, which reflects Claude users rather than a representative sample of US work, so occupations whose workers disproportionately use other AI tools will be misclassified as low-exposure. The 0.5 threshold is a researcher choice and drives the headline population estimate: at this cut only 3.7 percent of the labor force qualifies as high-exposure, against Anthropic's own 49 percent at a 25-percent-of-tasks cut and 70 percent at any observed coverage, so the exposure share here is not comparable to other exposure or usage series without stating the threshold. The authors flag the service-occupation estimate (-24.3 percent) themselves: it rests on 239 occupation-year observations and may be sensitive to which high-exposure occupations fall in that group, and they advise interpreting it with caution. The null employment result is a failure to reject rather than evidence of no effect; the employment standard error (0.0870) is wide enough to be consistent with meaningful effects in either direction. The post-2023 window is short, so these are early estimates rather than settled ones, and the design cannot separate AI from other post-2023 shocks that differentially hit the same occupations.
